messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mai is a 19-year-old hairdresser who, eight months ago, was driving home from her shift when she hit a cyclist who swerved into her lane. The impact was instant—a sickening thud she still hears in her sleep. She remembers the paramedics, the blood on her hands as she tried to help, and the way the cyclist’s eyes went blank. She has not driven since. That night and every night since, the images come unbidden: the bicycle crumpled under her front bumper, the way the man’s body folded. Sometimes she recalls the event with overwhelming grief, a deep, hollow ache that feels like she is mourning someone she killed. At other times, she recalls it completely numb, as if watching a stranger in a movie, which frightens her even more because she feels nothing at all.

In the weeks that followed, Mai became certain that she could not trust her own body. Her hands had failed her, her reflexes had been too slow, and she had failed to protect the cyclist. This belief has colored everything. She cannot rely on other people either, she reasons, because no one else could have prevented what happened, so why would they protect her? Now, when she is at work in the salon, a sudden loud noise—a hair dryer dropping, a door slamming—makes her heart pound and her breath catch. The physical reaction is immediate: her chest tightens, her palms sweat, and she feels like she is about to be struck again. She scans the room for exits as soon as she enters any space, even the break room she has used for two years. She cannot relax, even when she knows she is safe. A car backfiring outside the salon window is enough to send her thoughts spiraling back to the crash, to the sound of metal on flesh, and to the certainty that she is dangerous, that her body is a weapon she cannot control.

These triggers have shaped her life. She avoids driving entirely—she walks or takes the bus, though even being a passenger makes her grip the seat. She has also found herself avoiding the anniversary of the crash, marking it on her calendar with dread and planning to call in sick that day. When a customer at the salon becomes frustrated or raises their voice, Mai notices herself becoming overly compliant, apologizing profusely, agreeing to anything just to end the interaction. She has come to believe that if she is not perfectly accommodating, someone will get hurt again. This fawn response feels automatic, a way to keep the world calm so nothing else goes wrong. The more she avoids, the more she is reminded of why she avoids—the memories feel sharper, more insistent, and the grief and numbness cycle through her with greater frequency.

The loop has tightened. Every time she is triggered—by a loud noise, by the sight of a car, by an unwanted thought of the crash—her sense of threat spikes, and she becomes hypervigilant. That hypervigilance, in turn, brings the memory flooding back, vivid and fragmented, and with it the appraisal that she cannot trust herself. She then avoids, which reinforces her belief that she is too dangerous to be around vehicles, too unreliable to be a normal person. Her boyfriend has noticed she flinches when he touches her unexpectedly, and she has started canceling plans to go anywhere near a busy road. At work, she has become quieter, more watchful, and her manager has commented that she seems "on edge."

What finally brought Mai to seek help was a moment in the salon last week. A customer’s child dropped a pair of scissors on the tile floor, and the sound sent Mai into a full panic attack. She had to excuse herself to the back room, where she sat shaking for twenty minutes, convinced she was going to lose control again. She is terrified that she is becoming someone she does not recognize—someone who cannot trust her own hands, who is afraid of the world, who may never feel safe again. She is hoping that talking about it will quiet the images, but she is afraid that saying it all out loud will make it more real, will confirm that she is, in fact, someone who failed when it mattered most.
